1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to guard e5 and watch d4, and keeps both an open and a closed set-up available. The cost is the c6 square: the knight takes the place of the c-pawn, so the plan of ...c6 and ...d5 is gone.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward e4 and d5 and keeps the other knight and the central break in reserve. Black gets central space with the e5-pawn, White the extra tempo and pressure along the long diagonal, so the game resembles a Sicilian with the colours reversed.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre before the bishop reaches g2. After cxd5 Qxd5 the queen hits the rook on h1 along the long diagonal, so White must block it with a developing move, but the early queen then loses time to Nc3. Black trades the d-pawn for White's c-pawn and pays with tempi.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, so that after cxd5 the c-pawn recaptures and Black keeps two pawns in the centre. The move develops no piece, so White uses the time to develop and work against the black centre.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f2 and prepares castling. The set-up is sound, but the bishop can become a target for White's natural development, and White's long-diagonal bishop with a knight keeps an easy grip on d5.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which supports e5 along the long diagonal, for a closed game. The move is sound but commits Black to this set-up early, while White, a tempo ahead, can start queenside play.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 and frees the c8 bishop in a solid, waiting set-up. It concedes space and makes a later ...d5 cost another tempo, so White's long-diagonal bishop and queenside knight exert lasting pressure on d5.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly and prepares kingside castling. The move is sound but does nothing about the centre, and White builds a comfortable grip while Black still has to settle where the knights belong.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 for a Dutch-like attack with the e-pawn already on e5. It is a risky try rather than a refuted one: the h5-e8 diagonal and the e6 square are weakened, and White opens the centre with d4 and easy development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 h5.name: English Opening: Drill Variation
1.c4 e5 2.g3 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 to undermine the g3 pawn and open the h-file against the fianchetto. White simply develops and keeps a slight edge, while the advanced pawn loosens Black's kingside. It is playable but a gamble.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Moves the knight to the rim, aiming at c5 and b4, but leaves e5 without support and the centre to White. ...Nc5 costs two moves and can be hit by b4.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5, but blocks the f8 bishop and the e7 square and invites Nc3-d5 with tempo on the queen. White develops while the queen has little to do.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qf6.strategy: Defends e5, but takes the best square from the king's knight, and Nc3-d5 later hits the queen with a gain of time. White develops while the queen has to move again.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qg5.strategy: Eyes d2 and g3, but both are well protected, and 3.h4 chases the queen away at once. Black loses time with the queen for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, which keeps the c8-bishop shut in. White develops and can take the centre at ease.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Bb4.strategy: Puts the bishop on b4, where it attacks nothing because d2 is guarded. A move such as a3 or Nc3 forces it to commit or retreat, gaining time for White.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes f5 and g4 but does nothing about d5 or the centre. ...Nf6 does the same job with central influence.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ne7.strategy: Covers d5 and keeps c6 free for the c-pawn, but shuts in the f8-bishop, whose only open diagonal runs through e7, so a pawn or knight move is needed before it breathes. Sound, but clumsier than developing the other knight.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that only takes b5 away from White's pieces. Nothing is weakened beyond that, but White develops without resistance.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops b4, but costs a tempo and weakens b5, where a white knight can settle. The cost is small, and White develops without resistance.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 b6.strategy: Aims for ...Bb7, but with Bg2 coming the bishop hangs on the long diagonal until something blocks it. A slow flank move that weakens c6 and leaves White ahead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 c5.strategy: Takes d4 under control with the c-pawn, but leaves d5 as a lasting hole that White's pieces can occupy and press on, since no Black pawn can challenge it. A sound set-up, but Black has to develop carefully around that weakness.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 but blocks the king's knight, weakens e6 and the king's diagonal, and ties Black to passive defence. White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside and the long diagonal: after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the rook on h8 at once, and Black must block it. The kingside weaknesses stay for the rest of the game.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo to stop a Bg5 that is not yet possible, because the c1-bishop is blocked by the d2 pawn. Nothing is weakened, but White simply develops.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 e4.strategy: Advances the pawn without support to a square that White will soon attack with pieces and a pawn. Black can hold it only by spending more time defending it while White develops.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Qh4.strategy: Hangs the queen: the g3 pawn simply captures it with 3.gxh4.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good, blocks the f8 bishop and leaves the king in the centre for no reason. White develops and can open the position against the exposed king.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 wins a piece for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn: 3.cxb5 wins it, and Black has no lead in development or open lines in return.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at d5 and b7, so White presses on the centre from a distance without committing a pawn. The king's knight stays free, and White heads for a safe king and a flexible, strategic game.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Puts a second piece on d5 before the bishop arrives and leaves White the choice of square for the king's knight. The knight and the fianchetto work together against the centre and the game stays flexible; the cost is that the c3 knight gives Black's bishop a target.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and attacks e5, but invites ...e4, which gains space and drives the knight away. The knight finds a central post on d4, yet the advanced pawn cramps White before the bishop has joined the fight for the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5.strategy: The most direct answer to the fianchetto: Black challenges the c4 pawn and the long diagonal at once instead of waiting. The cost is that Black's centre dissolves after the exchange, and the e5 pawn becomes the target of White's development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: Develops and guards e5 while holding back the d-pawn, so Black avoids a direct fight over d5 and prepares a solid, compact set-up. White's bishop and c4 pawn keep their grip on d5, though, and Black must find a way to free the position later.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a pawn instead of a piece: the pawn guards d5 and stands on the long diagonal in front of the g2 bishop. Black builds a broad centre of pawns, at the cost of a move that develops nothing and takes c6 from the queen's knight.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the long diagonal onto d5: Black has to recapture, and the bishop on g2 now bears down on that square. Black's d-pawn is gone, and the game becomes one of piece play around the lone e5 pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, but allows ...e4, which hits the knight with gain of time. The knight must move, and c4 hangs to ...dxc4 as well, so White loses time and comes out behind in development.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.Nc3.strategy: Adds a second attacker on d5, but Black answers with a pawn push to d4 that hits the knight at once and gains space. The knight must find a new square, and White has spent a move to give Black a bigger share of the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which gains a central post. It is attacked by the bishop on g2 but defended by the queen, and Black keeps a healthy structure with e5 as its only advanced pawn, to be looked after as White develops.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Loses the queen for a bishop: the bishop on g2 takes it, and the knight on f6 recaptures. Black cannot afford to put the queen on a square attacked along the long diagonal.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 c6.strategy: A pawn offered for quick development: after White takes on c6, the knight recaptures with a move gained. But Black is a pawn down, and the bishop on g2 bears on the c6 knight and the b7 pawn behind it, so Black has no lead to pay for the material.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Develops with an attack on e5 and so forces Black to spend a move on defence. It blocks the bishop's diagonal for the moment, but the tempo is worth it: White gets the king's knight into play and keeps the initiative.

Challenges the centralised knight at once and brings a second piece into the centre while the bishop keeps the long diagonal open. If Black trades, White recaptures with a pawn and exchanges a sound structure for open lines; if the knight retreats, White has gained a useful move.

A quiet move that takes e4 from Black's pieces and frees the c1 bishop, while the g2 bishop and the c-pawn watch d5. It does not fight for the centre or attack e5, so Black has time to complete development and White's play is slower.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move and adds control of d4. The two knights give Black a compact, well-coordinated centre while White's bishop is still masked by its own knight.

Guards e5, but the bishop blocks the queen's protection of the knight on d5, so e4 hits the knight with tempo. The knight has a safe retreat, so little is lost, but White takes the centre with a gain of time.

Holds e5 with a pawn at a high price: it takes the f6 square from the knight and weakens the king on the diagonal leading to e8. Black spends a move on defence that develops nothing, while White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5..strategy: A quiet way to build the position: the pawn backs up e4, keeps Black's e-pawn from advancing with gain of space, and opens the c1 bishop. White does not hurry to castle and plays a patient manoeuvring game with the bishop on g2 watching the long diagonal.

Castles at once, tucking the king away behind the fianchetto while the f3 knight and the g2 bishop stay ready. White commits no central pawn yet and keeps the choice between queenside space-gaining play and a central break, with a safe king and a lasting initiative.

Hits the d5 knight, but Black simply trades. White recaptures with the b-pawn and is left with an isolated a-pawn, or with the d-pawn, after which Black trades queens with check and White loses the right to castle. The result is a drawish, slightly uncomfortable game for White.

Calm development that prepares castling and leaves the centre as it is. Black has no weaknesses: e5 is held by the knight, and the d5 knight is covered by the queen. The position is balanced, and the fight is for the long-term control of the central squares.

Sidesteps the centre before White can harass the d5 knight, and covers c4 and d5 from b6. Black accepts a slightly passive knight in exchange for a healthy structure and an easy path to castling, keeping the position solid.
Returns the knight to f6, where nothing can harass it. Black has spent extra time on the knight, but the position is solid and offers White no target, so the game stays balanced.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings a second piece to bear on d5, which is now covered by the c-pawn, the bishop and the knight, so ...d5 is hard to play. White has the more flexible choice for the other knight and builds slowly on the queenside and in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and attacks e5, but ...e4 gains space with tempo. The knight cannot go to d4, where ...Nxd4 wins a piece for a pawn, so it must go to g5 or back, and the advanced pawn cramps White. Black takes the initiative.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d3.strategy: Prepares a slow build-up: the pawn takes e4 from Black's pieces and frees the c1 bishop, while the g2 bishop and the c-pawn still watch d5. It does not yet fight for the centre, so Black has time to stake a claim there.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards d5 and e4. If Black takes on c3, White's pawns are doubled, at the price of giving up the bishop for a knight. Black fights actively for the centre rather than waiting for White to commit.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn, opens the c8 bishop and prepares castling. Black chooses a slow, solid structure and accepts that White keeps a hold on d5 and some extra space, in exchange for few weaknesses and no early commitments.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and so mirrors White's set-up. The bishop's diagonal is blocked by Black's own pieces for now, and Black does nothing about d5, so White keeps the grip on that square and the better space.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.N.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Closed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to the central post with tempo, hitting both the bishop and the f6 knight. If Black trades on d5, the recapture cxd5 chases the c6 knight. The result is a sharp, double-edged game, not a quiet one.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn, so that the c4 and e4 pawns together control d5 and give White a bind on that square. The price is that the bishop on g2 is blocked, and d4 is weakened. White builds a space advantage and plays for a slow squeeze.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Develops the king's knight and attacks e5, but leaves the c3 knight to the bishop. If Black takes it, either recapture doubles White's c-pawns, and White's compensation is the bishop pair. A flexible but quieter choice that gives up the initiative the sharper moves keep.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop, the straightforward reply. Black accepts that White has more space and the d5 square, and relies on a compact structure and active piece play to hold the balance.

Brings the king to safety first and keeps the options open: e5 is held by the knight, and the bishop can still trade on c3 when it suits. It leaves d6 undecided, so White gets time to settle the centre and strengthen the grip on d5.

Trades the bishop for the knight at once, doubling White's c-pawns whichever pawn recaptures. In return White gets the bishop pair and a strong pawn centre, though the g2 bishop is blocked by its own e4 pawn. Black's structure stays intact, and a slow manoeuvring game follows.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Closed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.strategy: Develops the knight to a square where it supports the c3 knight: if Black takes on c3, the knight recaptures and White's pawns stay intact. It also leaves the f-pawn free to advance, and prepares to challenge the centre in due course.

Supports e4 and frees the c1 bishop, but without the e2 knight to recapture, ...Bxc3+ forces White to take with a pawn and double the c-pawns. White gets the bishop pair and a half-open b-file in return, at the price of a damaged structure.

Develops and eyes e5, but leaves the c3 knight to ...Bxc3, when either recapture doubles White's c-pawns. White gets the bishop pair and a broad centre in return; the king's knight stands more actively than on e2, but the pawn structure is the price.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Closed Sicilian
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.e.strategy: Pins the e2 knight to the queen and threatens to trade the bishop for it, removing the only white piece that covers d4. Black develops outside the pawn chain with a clear aim, while White has to unpin or accept the exchange.

Brings the king to safety and finishes the kingside development before White's pieces coordinate. The chain of d6 and e5 holds the centre, and the bishop on b4 can still trade itself for the c3 knight or step back, so Black can wait and see what White intends.
Gives up the bishop for the knight even though the e2 knight can recapture, so White's pawns stay intact and White gets the bishop pair for free. Black has nothing concrete to show for it.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.d3.strategy: Backs up the e4 square and opens the c1 bishop, a patient move that fits the fianchettoed bishop. White plans to build slowly and avoids early weaknesses, so the game is likely to stay closed and manoeuvring for a long time.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the king's knight and eyes e5 at once, while the pawn moves that shape the centre wait. White keeps every set-up open and will castle soon, aiming for a slow manoeuvring game in which the pressure on e5 and d5 builds gradually.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.e3.strategy: Prepares the e2 square for the second knight and a central pawn break, a more direct plan than a slow d3. The cost is that the c1 bishop stays shut in until the d-pawn moves, and the pawn takes the e3 square from the bishop later.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.d3.strategy: Prepares castling and keeps the structure compact. The d6 pawn supports e5, so the bishop has no job to do in the centre, and Black has no weakness. A solid choice that keeps the game balanced and gives White the burden of finding a plan.

Fianchettoes the king's bishop to mirror White's set-up. The chain of d6 and e5 holds the centre, the king will be safe behind the bishop, and the game stays slow and balanced. The bishop has less scope on g7 while its own e5 pawn and the f6 knight stand in front of it.

Takes the b5 square away from White's knight and prepares queenside expansion against the c4 pawn. A useful but slow move that does nothing for development or the centre, so White keeps the freedom to choose a plan.
Develops the kingside knight, hits e5 and prepares castling. White settles for a slow manoeuvring game in which the fight is over the central squares, with a flexible fianchetto set-up.
Puts the bishop on a central diagonal that covers d4 and points at a7, but the f6 knight can attack it at once and the bishop has to move again. White spends a move for little gain.
Prepares a queenside space-gaining advance and takes b4 from Black's pieces. It is slow and useful, but does nothing for development or the centre, and Black can complete development at leisure.

1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.d3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with .. d6, Be7
1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.Nc3 d6 5.d3.strategy: Brings the king to safety. Black has a solid pawn chain of d6 and e5 against White's flexible set-up, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over the centre, each side looking for the right moment to change the structure.

Develops the last minor piece to an active square, where it eyes the c4 pawn and covers d5, so the white pawn chain feels pressure. The bishop can be hit by a knight from g5, which gains White a tempo, but Black's compact d6 and e5 structure stays sound.

Develops with an attack on the f3 knight, aiming to trade the bishop for it. If the exchange happens, Black gives up the bishop pair for a small gain in the centre. A sound but second-rate way to develop.
